lexical-retrieval.name: lexical retrieval
lexical-retrieval.definition: Ranking documents from overlap between query and document terms.
lexical-retrieval.explanation: Lexical retrievers operate on token identity and collection statistics. BM25 combines rare-term weighting, saturating term frequency, and document-length normalization. It is transparent and strong for names, codes, and quoted phrases, but misses paraphrases with no shared terms. Tokenization, stemming, stopword handling, corpus statistics, and parameter choices are part of the retrieval definition and must remain consistent between indexing and queries.

dense-retrieval.name: dense retrieval
dense-retrieval.definition: Ranking learned query and document vectors by similarity.
dense-retrieval.explanation: A dense retriever encodes text into fixed-width vectors and scores pairs with a dot product, cosine similarity, or distance. Those raw scores order candidates; they are not probabilities of relevance or calibrated support confidence. Training on labeled query-document pairs can bring paraphrases together even without exact term overlap. A word-table row and an averaged document embedding are different representations, even when they share the same width. The learned geometry depends on data and may blur rare identifiers. Search can be exact or approximate; embeddings alone do not determine the index algorithm.

context-assembly.name: context assembly
context-assembly.definition: Selecting and formatting retrieved evidence for an answerer.
context-assembly.explanation: Context assembly chooses chunks from retrieval results, orders them, enforces a context budget, and preserves stable source labels. The resulting evidence becomes input to an extractive reader or a generative language model. Poor chunk boundaries can omit qualifiers or mix sources. Source labels enable attribution checks, but a printed citation still needs a separate test that the passage supports the claim.

abstention.name: abstention
abstention.definition: Choosing not to answer when evidence or confidence is insufficient.
abstention.explanation: An abstention policy trades coverage for reliability. A retrieval system can reject questions when no known content appears, the best score is low, or the margin is ambiguous. Thresholds should be chosen on held-out answerable and unanswerable data, especially under domain shift. Reporting accuracy without coverage rewards systems that reject too much, while answering everything hides unsupported behavior and can turn weak retrieval into confident fabrication.

checks: BM25 ranks an exact-term fact first
Both query and document table gradients match direct-loss central differences
Training receives explicit labeled data and uses the documented learning rate
Dense exact search retrieves trained semantic pairs and held-out feature combinations
Changing retrieved fact text changes the extracted answer without retraining
Every answered fixture includes a matching source label
limitations: Three-document corpus and training pairs are too small for general retrieval claims
Dense vocabulary is fixed at construction and uses simple averaged word embeddings
Answerer is extractive and cannot synthesize across passages
Abstention thresholds are fixture-specific and uncalibrated
Known-term and score gates can accept unsupported questions containing familiar terms; extraction guarantees provenance, not relevance
